catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ambros:
Joseph Ambrose Stapf was a Tyrolean moral theologian whose textbooks trained Austrian seminarians for decades. Born at Fliess in the Upper Inn valley in 1785, he studied at Innsbruck and earned a doctorate in theology. He taught moral theology at Innsbruck and then at the Brixen seminary, where he also became a cathedral canon. He died at Brixen in 1844.

His chief work, a four-volume compendium of moral theology from 1827 to 1830, was praised for strict orthodoxy, clear order, and practical use. From 1830 it served as the official textbook for all Austrian seminaries. He later rewrote it in German and added works on Catholic education and on the life of St. Vincent de Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kulturkampf:
Kulturkampf names the political fight for the Catholic Church's rights and self-rule, fought chiefly in Prussia, then Baden, Hesse, and Bavaria. It burned hardest from 1871 to 1877 and eased from 1878 to 1891, pitting government, Liberals, and most Conservatives against bishops, priests, and most Catholic people.

The article traces three causes: party life in Germany, a mid-century drift of ideas, and Bismarck's European policy after 1870. Prussian Conservatives clung to the state's Protestant character and feared Catholic power through new parliaments. Liberals, once a narrow circle of professors and lawyers, drove the attack in the name of constitutional freedom against Rome.
